sections.normalized_html: According to the triangle inequality theorem, the sum of any two sides of a triangle must be greater than the length of the third side. Given that a triangle has side lengths of [MATH: 7] and [MATH: 10,] find the inequality that shows the possible lengths, [MATH: x,] of the third side.
sections.readable_text: According to the triangle inequality theorem, the sum of any two sides of a triangle must be greater than the length of the third side. Given that a triangle has side lengths of [MATH: 7] and [MATH: 10,] find the inequality that shows the possible lengths, [MATH: x,] of the third side.

sections.normalized_html:
We are told that, according to the triangle inequality theorem, the sum of any two sides of a triangle must be greater than the third side.

Applying the triangle inequality to the three combinations of side lengths, we obtain the following three inequalities: [MATH: 7 + 10|> x; 7 + x|> 10; 10 + x|> 7]

Now, we simplify each inequality: [MATH: x|< 17; x|> 3; x|> − 3]

Next, since side lengths are positive, the valid lower bound is [MATH: x > 3.] So, we have [MATH: 3 < x < 17.]

Therefore, the correct inequality is [MATH: 3 < x < 17.]
